device: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition
insight: softmax on RTX PRO 6000 (sm_120, large L2): output stores with an L2 evict_last cache-policy (createpolicy + st.global.L2::cache_hint; Triton eviction_policy='evict_last' lowers to the same) cut DRAM writes during the kernel from ~30 MB to ~11-15 MB and gave +2.7 to +3.7 SOL points; SOL tracked DRAM writes across all DSLs. The harness flags this as L2 flattering the timing, so treat gains as partly deferred write-back.

device: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition
insight: Persistent blocks that prefetch the next row into registers before the current row's reductions only pay off together with the evict_last store policy: with it 85.0 -> 92.4% (CUDA) and 83.1 -> 88.7% (Triton, tl.range num_stages=3); without it 79.5% (CUDA) and 76.2% (cuTile, which has no cache-policy control), below the one-row-per-block versions.

device: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition
insight: Getting 128-bit accesses needs DSL-specific alignment facts: CUDA prefetch loads must be coherent ld.global (ptxas sinks ld.global.nc past bar.sync); Triton needs tt.divisibility=16 attrs on the pointer args (tl.multiple_of had no effect) plus (cols//4)*4 for the row base; cuTile needs ArrayConstraint stride_constant/base_addr_divisible_by and ZERO padding (NEG_INF padding disables TMA); Warp only vectorizes aligned 2D shared tile_loads and needs its .meta smem_bytes as dynamic shared_mem in the manifest.
evidence: sass drafts t2/t3, c1-c3, w1-w2, v5; iters 2, 5, 7, 12

device: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition
insight: reduce on RTX PRO 6000: the large-n ceiling is ~86% of the DRAM roof (CUDA, Triton, Warp, cuTile all land 82-86%); Triton's persistent loop with unmasked full tiles (LDG.E.128) at 4 programs/SM was best (86.2%), while 8 blocks/SM in CUDA cost ~3 points. Pipelining with tl.range(num_stages=3) and LDGSTS did not help a pure streaming read.

device: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition
insight: Small reductions (<= 1 MB) bottom out at 4-6 us in every DSL against a 2.2 us empty-launch floor: one cold DRAM round trip plus an atomic is the real minimum, so ~40-55% of the launch roof is near the ceiling. cuTile adds a fixed ~8 us at small n (TMA and descriptor setup); size the grid to n (one block for n=4096) in CUDA.

device: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition
insight: nvcc turns plain loads through const float* __restrict__ into LDG.E.128.CONSTANT on its own, so removing __ldg changes nothing; check the SASS with --show LDG before spending an iteration on a load-path change. Warp vectorizes only aligned 2D shared tile_loads: pass the input twice, as a 1D array for the tail and a [n/TILE, TILE] view for full tiles.

device: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition
insight: Scan: never form an exclusive prefix as inclusive minus the element's own value; with mixed magnitudes the subtraction cancels small earlier sums (failed adversarial checks at 6.9e-4). Shift the inclusive prefix by one lane (shfl_up 1) in CUDA, or scan the input loaded at offs - 1 in Triton.

device: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition
insight: CUDA single-pass decoupled look-back scan: warp-parallel look-back (32 predecessors per round, ballot for the nearest full prefix) and 16 items per thread took it from 58% to 62%; 64M sits near 79% of the read+write roof. A 3-pass Triton reduce-then-scan reads the input twice and loses at 64M (56%) but wins at 4M (67%) because the second read of a 16 MB input hits L2.

device: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition
insight: Dispatching sizes across DSLs in one manifest (when + per-launch source) beat every single-DSL candidate: CUDA single-pass below 1M and from 16M, the Triton 3-pass in between (64.7% vs 62.4%). cuTile and Warp were not tried for scan: a single pass needs inter-block spinning, which neither expresses well.

device: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition
insight: Triton loses alignment facts through control flow: assigning base and mask in if/else branches and loading after the if left sizePerThread=[1] and scalar LDG.E; calling an inlined @triton.jit helper inside each branch restored LDG.E.128. Module-level constants in Triton kernels must be tl.constexpr(...) objects (a plain float or an annotation is a NameError).

device: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition
insight: Softmax with the row in registers (read once, write once) is the shape that matters: 57.5% -> 74% from the baseline in one step. Warp-per-row wins for many short rows (4096x512 at 87%), Triton's program-per-row for a few short rows (64x1024), and long rows (4096 to 16384 cols) sit at ~82% of DRAM in both CUDA and Triton. A mid shape like 1024x1024 (8 MB, ~8 us) stays near 57%: it pays both the latency floor and the transfer, and the roof only counts the larger.

device: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition
insight: FP32 SGEMM on RTX PRO 6000 (sm_120): 128x128 block tile, 8x8 outputs per thread, double-buffered 8-deep slabs and interleaved fragments (tx*4 and 64+tx*4) reached 40.7% of the FP32 peak at 4096^3; the interleaving (no 2-way bank conflicts) was worth more than double buffering (+2.7 vs +1.2 points). Small and mid shapes need the tile chosen from the shape (128 / 64 / 16 by blocks per SM): 256^3 went from 9% to 36%.

device: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition
insight: FP32 attention (D=64) on sm_120: a fused online-softmax kernel with one thread per query, q and the accumulator in registers (254 regs) and K/V tiles broadcast from shared memory went from 1% to ~31% of FP32 peak at S=2048-4096 (22.9% overall). Splitting a query across two threads (143 regs) was worse (17.6%): duplicated exp2 and softmax bookkeeping per key cost more than the extra occupancy gained.

device: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition
insight: Triton FP32 FlashAttention (ieee dots): 64x64 tiles with 4 warps spilled (391 LDL, 255 STL at 255 regs) and ran at 7%; 64x32 with 8 warps fit in 92 regs without spills and reached 15%, still below the CUDA one-thread-per-query kernel.
